implementation_notes: Ruby's Array carries the destructive selection family, so the idiom is a method call: delete_if { |x| ... } removes every element for which the block is true (reject! is its synonym), while select! (alias filter!) and keep_if do the opposite and keep the elements the block accepts; all of them mutate the receiver in place, preserve the order of the survivors, and return the receiver. The non-bang select/reject/filter stay copy-out, and the compaction itself is the interpreter's job, which is why the two-step algorithm-plus-erase structure does not appear. Use the bang forms when the array is the value you intend to keep mutating, and the non-bang forms when the array is shared or frozen, since mutation of a shared array is visible to every reference.
code_sketch:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
nums.delete_if { |n| n.even? }    # => [1, 3, 5], same object
nums.keep_if { |n| n > 3 }        # => [5], the complement
kept = nums.reject { |n| n > 4 }  # copy-out alternative
pitfalls: reject! and select! return nil when nothing was removed while delete_if and keep_if return the array: chaining (arr.reject! { ... }.map) breaks exactly when the predicate matched nothing - the documented difference between these synonyms.

delete(value) removes every occurrence of a value, but delete_at(i) removes one position and shifts the tail per call, so a delete_at loop is the O(n*k) anti-pattern the destructive selection methods replace.
Mutating the array inside the block or while an Enumerator is mid-traversal raises RuntimeError or skips elements, and any bang method on a frozen array raises FrozenError.
delete_if scans once per call, so applying k criteria as k calls costs k passes: fuse them into one block when the predicate is cheap.
sources: docs.ruby-lang.org, class Array (Ruby 3.3) - 'Destructive Selection': select! and reject! are the destructive counterparts of select and reject, and delete_if and keep_if have the exact opposite result for the same block (arr.delete_if { |a| a < 4 } leaves [4, 5, 6]): https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/3.3/Array.html
